item.text:
The sources support this bottom line: there is no shared view that `robots.txt` means one thing. The standards baseline treats it as an advisory signal, several crawler operators operationalize it as a practical opt-out or even a default-permission system, and some publishers try to give it contractual or copyright-reservation weight while others call it an inadequate or misleading opt-out mechanism. [(RFC 9309)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309) [(Google robots.txt guide)](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) [(OpenAI crawlers)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots) [(Anthropic crawler help)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8896518-does-anthropic-crawl-data-from-the-web-and-how-can-site-owners-block-the-crawler) [(Common Crawl FAQ)](https://commoncrawl.org/faq) [(News/Media Alliance comments, 2023)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Final-NMA-USCO-AI-NOI-Response-Submitted-10.30.23.pdf) [(AP terms)](https://www.ap.org/terms-and-conditions/)

**Supported fact**
- RFC 9309 says crawlers are “requested to honor” the rules in `robots.txt` and says those rules “are not a form of access authorization,” which is the clearest standards-level statement that `robots.txt` is not itself permissioning or authentication. [(RFC 9309)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309)
- Google’s documentation aligns with that view: it says `robots.txt` is mainly for managing crawl traffic, “cannot enforce crawler behavior,” is not a way to keep pages secure, and blocked URLs can still appear in Google Search results. [(Google robots.txt guide)](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro)
- Google nevertheless uses `robots.txt` as a product control surface: `Google-Extended` lets publishers manage whether Google-crawled content may be used for future Gemini training and grounding, while Google says that control does not affect ordinary Google Search inclusion. [(Google common crawlers)](https://developers.google.com/crawling/docs/crawlers-fetchers/google-common-crawlers)
- OpenAI says site owners can use separate `robots.txt` tokens to allow search while disallowing training, and says disallowing `GPTBot` indicates content “should not be used” for training. It also says `ChatGPT-User` requests may fall outside `robots.txt` because they are user-initiated rather than automatic crawling. [(OpenAI crawlers)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots)
- Anthropic says its bots honor `robots.txt`, says disabling `ClaudeBot` signals that future materials “should be excluded” from model-training datasets, and says opting out requires modifying `robots.txt`. [(Anthropic crawler help)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8896518-does-anthropic-crawl-data-from-the-web-and-how-can-site-owners-block-the-crawler)
- Common Crawl says `CCBot` will stop crawling when blocked in `robots.txt`, says it periodically re-checks `robots.txt`, and elsewhere says that, by default, absence of blocking rules is interpreted as permission to crawl. [(Common Crawl FAQ)](https://commoncrawl.org/faq) [(Common Crawl AIO post)](https://commoncrawl.org/blog/ai-optimization-is-here-are-you-ready-for-search-2-0)

**Disagreement**
- Publisher-side sources do not agree with the “no block means yes” framing: the News/Media Alliance said some commenters had argued that publishers consented by not opting out via `robots.txt`, and NMA called that a “false choice.” [(News/Media Alliance comments, 2022)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/NMA-2nd-Round-Comments-CO-Final.pdf)
- The same trade group later argued that publishers should not have to affirmatively opt out of AI scraping, called opt-out “antithetical” to U.S. copyright principles, said `robots.txt` is voluntary and often ignored, and described it as a “blunt tool” that forces a choice between authorizing all uses and authorizing none. [(News/Media Alliance comments, 2023)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Final-NMA-USCO-AI-NOI-Response-Submitted-10.30.23.pdf)
- News/Media Alliance also told Common Crawl in April 2026 that no copyright holder is required to opt out of unauthorized copying, and asked Common Crawl to state publicly that it cannot authorize downstream use of scraped publisher content. [(NMA letter to Common Crawl, Apr. 29, 2026)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Letter-to-Common-Crawl-4.29.2026.pdf)
- AP’s public terms take a different tack: AP says users agree to comply with instructions in `robots.txt`, and AP labels those terms a “legally binding agreement,” which is an explicit attempt to give `robots.txt` contractual significance. [(AP terms)](https://www.ap.org/terms-and-conditions/)
- A publisher-adjacent dissenting voice, Jeff Jarvis, told the Senate that technology companies already offer “simple opt-out mechanisms (see: robots.TXT),” showing that even within journalism-policy debates there is not a single publisher-side position. [(Jarvis testimony)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/01/Jeff-Jarvis-Testimony.pdf)

**Standards-participant disagreement**
- The active IETF AIPREF draft says preferences can express “restrictions or permissions,” can be used in jurisdictions with or without legal obligations, but also says the draft does not ensure preferences are followed and that legal arrangements may override machine-readable preferences; the same draft says its text does not yet reflect full WG consensus. [(AIPREF vocab draft)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab/)
- The IETF AI Preferences charter describes the work as expressing and attaching “preferences,” not as creating access control. [(AIPREF charter)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/charter-ietf-aipref/)
- In the IAB AI-CONTROL workshop report, participants said `robots.txt` “cannot be the only solution to opt-out,” which shows active standards participants see it as useful but insufficient. [(RFC 9969)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc9969/)
- Meeting minutes show unresolved disagreement inside the standards process: one participant said `robots.txt` “state[s] the preference,” another said `robots.txt` is “about access control rather than usage,” and others argued it is where bots already look but “not enough on its own.” Meeting minutes are evidence of discussion, not IETF consensus. [(AIPREF interim minutes, Apr. 8, 2025)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/minutes-interim-2025-aipref-01-202504080715/) [(IETF 122 AIPREF minutes)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/minutes-122-aipref/)

**Legal significance**
- U.S. case law in the sources does not support a clean rule. In `hiQ v. LinkedIn`, the Ninth Circuit described `robots.txt` as a widely used standard for stating bot-behavior rules and said adherence is voluntary. [(hiQ v. LinkedIn)](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/17-16783/17-16783-2022-04-18.html)
- In December 2025, the Southern District of New York held in `Ziff Davis v. OpenAI` that `robots.txt` files are not DMCA measures that “effectively control access,” characterizing them as requests rather than real access controls. [(Ziff Davis v. OpenAI)](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/new-york/nysdce/1%3A2025cv04315/643043/300/)
- That same opinion said `Healthcare Advocates` involved a “unique factual circumstance” where a user would actually have been prevented from viewing archived content through the Wayback Machine, which implies that any legal significance may depend heavily on context rather than on `robots.txt` alone. [(Ziff Davis v. OpenAI)](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/new-york/nysdce/1%3A2025cv04315/643043/300/)

**Inference**
- The best-supported synthesis is that the dispute is not just semantic. Different actors are trying to use the same file for at least three different jobs: courtesy signaling, product-specific traffic or training controls, and evidence for contractual or copyright-reservation arguments. That inference follows from RFC 9309, crawler docs, publisher submissions, and AP’s terms. [(RFC 9309)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9309) [(OpenAI crawlers)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots) [(Anthropic crawler help)](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/8896518-does-anthropic-crawl-data-from-the-web-and-how-can-site-owners-block-the-crawler) [(Common Crawl FAQ)](https://commoncrawl.org/faq) [(News/Media Alliance comments, 2023)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Final-NMA-USCO-AI-NOI-Response-Submitted-10.30.23.pdf) [(AP terms)](https://www.ap.org/terms-and-conditions/)

**Uncertainty**
- There is good evidence that major operators document how they treat `robots.txt`, but much weaker evidence that all crawlers actually comply in practice; Google itself says not all crawlers obey `robots.txt`, and NMA says some AI developers respect it while others do not. [(Google robots.txt guide)](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/robots/intro) [(News/Media Alliance comments, 2023)](https://www.newsmediaalliance.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/02/Final-NMA-USCO-AI-NOI-Response-Submitted-10.30.23.pdf)
- There is also no strong evidence in these sources for a universal legal rule that `robots.txt` either always creates permission, always negates permission, or always has no legal effect. The sources instead show context-specific contract drafting, unsettled standards work, and mixed judicial treatment. [(AP terms)](https://www.ap.org/terms-and-conditions/) [(Ziff Davis v. OpenAI)](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/new-york/nysdce/1%3A2025cv04315/643043/300/) [(hiQ v. LinkedIn)](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/ca9/17-16783/17-16783-2022-04-18.html) [(AIPREF vocab draft)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-aipref-vocab/)

**Lack of good evidence**
- I did not find a primary-source, cross-industry standard or court opinion in these materials saying that the mere absence of a `robots.txt` restriction universally grants legal permission to crawl or train. The closest thing in the sources is operator-specific practice, especially Common Crawl’s statement that it treats absence of blocking as permission for `CCBot`. [(Common Crawl AIO post)](https://commoncrawl.org/blog/ai-optimization-is-here-are-you-ready-for-search-2-0)
